title: Nilekani Urges India to Become the AI Use-Case Capital, Not Chase Chip Dominance
excerpt: The Infosys co-founder says India's strength lies in scaling AI to a billion people through diffusion, not competing in the model-building race.
body:
• Nandan Nilekani argues India should focus on becoming the "use case capital of the world" rather than competing to build AI chips or foundational models
  • A global coalition including Anthropic, Google, the Gates Foundation and UNDP launched the "100 Diffusion Pathways by 2030" initiative at the India AI Impact Summit 2026
  • Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei revealed that Claude usage for programming in India has doubled in four months, with the company deepening its focus on Indic languages

Nandan Nilekani, co-founder of Infosys and the architect of Aadhaar, has laid out a clear strategic vision for India's role in the global AI race: stop chasing chip supremacy and start deploying artificial intelligence at population scale.

Speaking at a fireside chat with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei during the India AI Impact Summit 2026 in New Delhi, Nilekani argued that India's competitive advantage lies not in building the largest AI models but in getting technology into the hands of a billion people.

The Diffusion Argument

"I have always been saying that India should focus on becoming the use case capital of the world," Nilekani told the summit audience. He drew on India's track record with Aadhaar and UPI to make the case that technology diffusion is fundamentally different from technology creation.

"Diffusion is both an art and a science. It involves institutions, policymaking, negotiations, dealing with incumbents, dealing with newcomers, the whole trust-building thing," he said. "If all the investments in AI are going to deliver value to society, not just to individuals, we'll have to look at diffusion pathways."

The Infosys chairman warned that without deliberate effort to spread AI's benefits broadly, a backlash is inevitable. He pointed to globalisation's uneven track record as a cautionary tale.

"The resentment of the blue-collar worker led to the train wreck of globalisation. The resentment of the white-collar worker is going to lead to the train wreck of AI."

— Nandan Nilekani, Co-founder, Infosys

100 Diffusion Pathways by 2030

A centrepiece of the summit was the launch of the "100 Diffusion Pathways by 2030" initiative, a global coalition that includes Anthropic, Google, the Gates Foundation and the United Nations Development Programme. The initiative aims to create open playbooks for scaling AI applications across sectors including education, healthcare and agriculture.

Nilekani described a diffusion pathway as a packaged method to reach a particular goal, incorporating technical guardrails, institutional buy-in and data strategies. He cited the Maharashtra Agri-stack, known as Mahavistar, as a working example — a system that uses AI to assist 2.6 million dairy farmers in caring for their cattle through a conversational bot.

Anthropic's India Bet

Amodei offered his own bullish assessment of India's AI potential. He revealed that Anthropic is deepening its engagement with the country, including through a newly announced partnership with Infosys.

"The fraction of Claude usage for technical programming and software engineering is substantially higher here in India than it is in most other places in the world," Amodei said. "The use of Claude and Claude Code has doubled in India in just four months."

He added that Anthropic's latest model, Sonnet 4.6, features significantly improved performance across 10 Indic languages — a move aimed at expanding AI access beyond English-speaking users.

A Pragmatic Vision

Amodei speculated during the conversation whether AI could push India to a 20 or even 25 percent growth rate by combining its technical workforce with its massive population. Nilekani's response was characteristically grounded.

"I don't know about 25 percent. If I get 10 percent, I'll be happy," he said. "The focus has to be on inclusion. This AI has to work for people, starting from the user and how we can improve their lives."

The summit, which also featured remarks from India's IT Secretary on keeping humans in the loop with AI systems, comes at a moment when a separate report urged India to build "strategic agency" in AI rather than pursuing autonomy from foreign technology. The report argued that India's digital public infrastructure — from UPI to Aadhaar — already gives it a unique foundation to deploy AI applications at a scale that few other countries can match.

For the Indian diaspora, the implications are significant. If Nilekani's vision takes hold, India's tech sector would pivot from being a back-office for Western AI companies to becoming the proving ground for how AI can reach the world's most underserved populations — a model that could be exported to the Global South and reshape how the technology industry values scale over sophistication.
